planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun, spacing plants far enough apart to show off the airy, spidery plumes without crowding.

directions: One of the older German-bred maiden grass selections, Silberspinne forms a dense, upright clump of narrow, arching green leaves that stays noticeably smaller and more refined than large-statured cultivars like Silberfeder or Gracillimus. In late summer, slender flower stalks rise well above the foliage carrying tight, pink-tinged tassels that mature into fine, silvery, spider-web-like plumes, an effect that gives the cultivar both its German name and its airy, delicate winter presence. Foliage shifts to warm gold tones in autumn before the whole clump is cut back hard in late winter, and congested clumps benefit from division every three to four years.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun with room for the plumes to drape outward as they mature; consistent moisture during the first season speeds establishment.

directions: Kaskade is grown chiefly for its abundant, gracefully drooping rose-pink plumes, which emerge in mid to late summer well above a tall, upright clump of arching green foliage and gradually cascade outward as they age, giving the cultivar its cascade-inspired name. As the plumes mature through fall they fade from pink to a shimmering silvery white, remaining attractive and structurally sound into winter. The strong, upright habit resists flopping despite the heavy plume display, making it a good choice as a specimen or back-of-border accent. Cut the entire clump to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Grosse Fontane Maiden Grass (Big Fountain Miscanthus)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun with ample room to reach its large mature size; site as a specimen or screen rather than in a tight border.

directions: Grosse Fontane is a large, vigorous maiden grass valued for its fountain-shaped, gracefully arching clump of green foliage and its light, airy plumes, which open reddish in mid-summer, well earlier than many full-size Miscanthus sinensis selections, before fading to silver as autumn progresses. Reaching up to 8 feet in flower, it is best used as a bold specimen, screen, or backdrop planting where its billowing form has room to develop fully. The persistent plumes and foliage provide strong winter structure until the clump is cut back hard in late winter ahead of new spring growth.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun with generous room on all sides; this is one of the largest maiden grass selections and needs space to reach full size without crowding.

directions: True to its name, Goliath is among the largest of the maiden grass cultivars, forming a massive upright clump of thick stems and broad, cascading green leaves that can reach 8 to 10 feet tall, occasionally more in favorable conditions. Reddish-brown plumes emerge in late summer well above the foliage mass, aging to a warm silvery tan and persisting into winter, while the broad leaves turn yellow-gold in autumn. Its imposing scale makes it best suited to large properties, screening, or as a dramatic single specimen rather than a typical mixed border. Cut the entire clump to the ground in late winter before new shoots emerge.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in full sun; site where the smoky plume color and strong autumn foliage tones can be viewed at close range.

directions: Gewitterwolke, German for thundercloud, takes its name from the smoky, purple-gray cast of its emerging flower plumes, which appear in late summer above an upright clump of narrow green foliage before aging toward silver. The cultivar is especially noted for its strong, reliable autumn foliage color, turning rich shades of orange and copper well before many other Miscanthus sinensis selections color up, giving it a distinct two-season ornamental role. Its mid-sized habit fits more readily into a mixed border than the largest maiden grass cultivars. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes, dividing congested clumps every three to four years.
